context_blurb:
Gravity is the pull that every mass has on every other. It makes a dropped pen fall, holds the Moon on its path round Earth and keeps space stations circling overhead. Isaac Newton set out its law in 1687, in his great book the Principia.

Any two masses pull on each other equally hard, and bigger masses pull harder. So two bowling balls do tug on each other, but far too weakly to notice; only a mass as huge as a planet gives a pull you can feel. Henry Cavendish measured such a tiny pull between lead balls in 1797 and 1798, with a balance so delicate that he shut it in a case and read it through a telescope from outside.

A world's pull comes from its mass, and the Moon has only about one eighty-first of Earth's; being smaller also puts its surface nearer its centre, so the pull there is about a sixth of Earth's. That is why a pack that weighs an astronaut down at home rides lightly on the Moon.

Mass is the amount of matter in a thing, the same anywhere; weight is gravity's pull on it, which changes from world to world. Say a rock reads 2 kilograms on a spring scale and on a pan balance at home. On the Moon, the rock and the metal masses on the balance's other pan are both pulled about six times less, so the balance still reads 2 kilograms. The spring scale feels only the rock's weight, so it reads about a sixth as much, roughly a third of a kilogram.

A pull weakens with distance, yet gravity has no edge. As a probe coasts toward Mars, Earth's pull on it grows weaker and weaker, but it never ends. Far out, the Sun's stronger pull adds to Earth's rather than blocking it, and gravity needs no air: Earth's pull holds the Moon far beyond the air.

Near Earth, distance matters less than most people guess. The International Space Station flies about 400 km up, which takes it only from about 6,400 to 6,800 km from Earth's centre. Up there Earth's pull is still about nine-tenths as strong as at the ground, nearly as strong as down here.

Earth is some 81 times as massive as the Moon, so halfway to the Moon Earth still pulls a coasting craft 81 times as hard as the Moon does. The two pulls match only much nearer the Moon than Earth, about nine-tenths of the way, and past that point the Moon's pull wins.

Newton also saw how a thing can circle Earth without ever landing. He imagined a cannon on a very tall mountain, firing level, and asked us to picture Earth with no air. Each ball curves down to the ground, a faster one landing farther off; throw a ball level, softly and then hard, to see it. Fire one fast enough, Newton reasoned, and it would circle Earth. It still falls the whole time, but it moves forward so fast that the round Earth curves away beneath it as quickly as it drops. An orbit is a fall that never ends, and no push from the blast is needed to keep the ball going.

The space station, its crew and everything aboard are falling toward Earth in just that way, all the time, and since they all fall together, an astronaut's pen hangs beside her instead of dropping to the floor. Gravity has not gone, and NASA calls the phrase 'zero gravity' misleading.

An orbit can also fail. America's first space station, Skylab, circled empty after 1974, brushed by wisps of thin air. Slowed a little, it fell toward Earth slightly faster than the round Earth curved away beneath it, so it sank lower, into thicker air that slowed it still more. On 11 July 1979 it fell back through the atmosphere, scattering pieces across the Indian Ocean and Western Australia. The International Space Station sinks the same way, about 2 km a month, so docked spacecraft fire their engines to push it back up.
